questions.question: In a diagonalization $A=PDP^{-1}$, what kind of matrix is $D$?
What do the diagonal entries of $D$ represent in $A=PDP^{-1}$?
options: Entries of the first column of $P$

questions.question: What do the columns of $P$ represent in a diagonalization?
Why does diagonalization make the action of a linear map simpler?
options: It replaces multiplication by addition of rows.
It turns every vector into the zero vector.
In an eigenbasis, the map scales coordinates separately.

questions.question: When is a diagonal matrix already diagonalized?
options: Only if every diagonal entry is $1$.
Never; diagonal matrices cannot be diagonalized.

questions.question: If $A=P\operatorname{diag}(1,4)P^{-1}$, what are the eigenvalues listed by this diagonalization?
If the first column of $P$ in $A=PDP^{-1}$ is $v_1$ and the first diagonal entry of $D$ is $5$, what equation does $v_1$ satisfy?
If $A=P\operatorname{diag}(2,7)P^{-1}$, what is $A^2$?
For $A=\operatorname{diag}(-1,3)$, which diagonalization is immediate?
If $P$ has dependent columns, can it serve as the change-of-basis matrix in a diagonalization?
options: No, because $P$ would not be invertible.
Yes, because dependent columns are easier to diagonalize.

questions.question: Why are eigenvectors placed in the columns of $P$ rather than chosen arbitrarily?
options: The columns of $P$ are the diagonal entries of $D$.
The equation $AP=PD$ records $Av_i=λ_iv_i$ column by column.
The columns of $P$ must be standard basis vectors only.

questions.question: Why is $A=PDP^{-1}$ equivalent to $P^{-1}AP=D$?
options: Multiplying by $P^{-1}$ on the left and by $P$ on the right converts one equation into the other.
The equivalence requires $D$ to be singular.
They are different definitions with unrelated meanings, irrespective of the particular case.

questions.question: Why does diagonalization make computing $A^{k}$ easy?
options: The eigenvalues are replaced by row operations.
The power of every diagonal matrix is zero.

questions.question: Let $D=\operatorname{diag}(3,-2)$. What is $D^3$?
Suppose $P=[v_1\ v_2]$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(2,5)$, and $A=PDP^{-1}$. What is $Av_2$?
If $A=P\operatorname{diag}(0,2)P^{-1}$, what is $A^3$?
What can go wrong if the eigenvectors used as columns of $P$ do not form a basis?
options: $P$ is not invertible, so the diagonalization is invalid.
The eigenvalues cease to be roots of the characteristic polynomial.
The matrix $D$ stops being diagonal automatically.

questions.question: Why does the order of the columns of $P$ matter only together with the order of the diagonal entries of $D$?
options: Changing the order of columns always destroys invertibility.
Each eigenvector column must be paired with its corresponding eigenvalue.
The diagonal entries of $D$ must be sorted from small to large.
The order never matters, even if the pairings are changed.

questions.question: If $A=P\operatorname{diag}(2,-1,4)P^{-1}$, what is $A^0$?
A claimed diagonalization uses $P=[(1,0)^T\ (2,0)^T]$. What is the problem?
options: The two columns are dependent, so $P$ is not invertible.
The matrix $P$ has too many columns.
The columns are both nonzero, so there is no problem.
The diagonal entries of $D$ must both be zero.
